headline: Patient-safety learning with generative AI, and why AI did not rescue tired residents' chest X-ray reads
intro: This briefing looks at AI and trainees from two sides. A survey links how students use generative AI to their self-reported safety practice, and a small reader study tested whether AI help can make up for radiology residents' fatigue after a night shift.

items.title: Generative AI Factors, Cognitive Engagement, and Patient Safety Learning in Medical Education: Mixed Methods Study
items.summary: The researchers first interviewed 8 clerkship students who use generative AI. They then surveyed 214 students from 5 private universities in the Jakarta Metropolitan Area, Indonesia, to test a model of how AI-related factors relate to self-reported infection-prevention practice on the wards. Students' confidence in using AI output (self-efficacy, β=0.477) and their sense of balanced control over the AI (β=0.407) were both linked to better self-reported practice, together explaining 51.9% of its variance. Overall model fit was limited, and because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the authors say they do not establish causal or clinical effects; no actual safety outcomes were observed.
items.why_it_matters: The authors suggest clerkship guidance should cover supervised checking of AI output, protecting patient data, following local protocols, and keeping clinicians responsible for clinical decisions. Educators should treat this as a hypothesis to test, not proof that AI training improves patient safety.

items.title: From dusk till dawn?—Night shift-induced fatigue, diagnostic performance, and AI assistance in chest radiography
items.summary: The task was reading bedside chest radiographs for five findings: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion, pulmonary opacities and atelectasis. Residents read with and without help from an AI model built at Aachen University Hospital, which pre-filled a structured report that they could accept or change. Ten radiology residents (mean experience 35 months) each read sets of 33 radiographs before and after a first-call on-site night shift, and the morning after the shift they read both with and without AI. Accuracy was measured as Cohen's κ against an expert majority vote. Six residents classed as fatigued by eye tracking fell from κ = 0.71 ± 0.05 to κ = 0.61 ± 0.10 after the shift (p < 0.001), and non-fatigued readers fell from κ = 0.72 ± 0.03 to κ = 0.65 ± 0.03 (p = 0.037). AI help did not significantly improve accuracy (Δκ = 0.03–0.04; p ≥ 0.525) and did not restore pre-shift performance, although it significantly shortened reporting time in non-fatigued readers (Δ9.9 s; p = 0.031). The main limitation is size: 10 residents at a single centre, using one in-house AI model on a set of test radiographs rather than live clinical reporting.
items.why_it_matters: A tired resident's accuracy can drop while reading speed stays the same, so neither the resident nor a supervisor may notice. This study suggests that a pre-filled AI report alone does not fix the problem. Educators and programme leads should not count on AI as a substitute for fatigue management and supervision overnight.
